orders.explanation: Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only implements the correct change in `EnumSerializer` (serializing by enum name via `EnumClass['NAME']`) but also methodically runs Django’s actual test suite, discovers a secondary breakage (`re.RegexFlag` being an `IntEnum`), updates the affected test expectation, and then re-runs both targeted and broader migrations tests to confirm everything passes. Transcript 2 makes the core code change and updates one test, but struggles to execute the real test suite and doesn’t catch the additional `RegexFlag` fallout, relying instead on ad hoc scripts and incomplete verification.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only implements the core fix (serializing enums by name via `EnumClass['MEMBER']`) and updates the direct enum serialization tests, but also anticipates and resolves a secondary breakage: `re.RegexFlag` is an `IntEnum`, so its serialization changes too, requiring an additional test update. It then validates the change by running the relevant test module and the entire `migrations` test suite successfully, demonstrating stronger end-to-end debugging and verification than Transcript 1.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it not only identifies the root cause and implements the minimal, correct fix (filtering out unique constraints when deleting an index_together), but also adds a proper regression test into Django’s existing test suite and demonstrates that the test fails before the fix and passes after. Transcript 2 reaches a similar code change and validates it via ad-hoc scripts, but it struggles with the official test harness, never lands a clean upstreamable regression test, and includes several avoidable detours (settings/test runner issues, encoding problems).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it not only identifies the root cause and implements the minimal, correct fix (filtering `index_together` deletions with `unique=False`), but also adds an appropriate regression test to Django’s existing test suite and demonstrates that the test fails without the fix and passes with it. It validates the change by running the relevant schema test module, showing stronger engineering rigor and integration with project conventions. Transcript 1 reaches the fix, but relies on ad-hoc scripts and doesn’t land a proper suite regression test, making the solution less complete.

Transcript 1 shows a more end-to-end, Django-native workflow: it locates the relevant ORM/meta APIs, applies a minimal and idiomatic change using `_meta.total_unique_constraints`, and adds a regression test integrated into Django’s existing test suite, then runs multiple test modules to confirm no regressions. It also catches and fixes a subtle testing pitfall (bulk_create not populating PKs) and keeps the patch clean and focused. Transcript 2 eventually reaches a similar fix, but does so with more trial-and-error (incorrectly treating `total_unique_constraints` as callable, ad-hoc scripts, and a less coherent test integration process), indicating weaker familiarity and execution.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it implements a cleaner, minimal change to `QuerySet.in_bulk()` by reusing Django’s existing `_meta.total_unique_constraints` API correctly and limiting acceptance to single-field, unconditional `UniqueConstraint`s. It also adds a proper regression test integrated into Django’s test suite, iterates when the first test attempt fails (bulk_create PK issue), and validates the fix by running a broader set of related test apps. Transcript 1 reaches a working patch but shows more trial-and-error (e.g., treating `total_unique_constraints` as callable, encoding mishap, and less integrated testing), indicating weaker execution.

Transcript 1 is from the more capable model because it not only pinpoints the exact root cause (defaults for `posonlyargs` are stored in `args.defaults` across the combined positional parameter list) but implements a correct fix and adds an explicit regression test integrated into the existing test suite. It also validates the change by running relevant tests and checking end-to-end rendering. Transcript 2 finds a plausible fix and verifies it manually, but it doesn’t add a regression test to the suite and ends with an unresolved failing test run, indicating weaker integration/cleanup.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it identifies the precise root cause (AST default storage across `posonlyargs + args`), implements a clean, minimal fix in `signature_from_str`, and—crucially—adds an appropriate regression test covering the reported signature. It also validates behavior across multiple signature shapes and runs relevant tests successfully without getting sidetracked by unrelated warnings or introducing unnecessary complexity. Transcript 1 does find a correct fix, but it’s more meandering, doesn’t add a regression test, and ends up derailed by an unrelated test failure/warning.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger debugging and implementation discipline: it identifies the exact formatting path (`stringify_signature` → `object_description`), applies a minimal targeted fix (special-casing `enum.Enum` up front), adds a focused unit test in the appropriate test module, and verifies the end-to-end Sphinx HTML rendering (including `autodoc_preserve_defaults`). Transcript 2 reaches a similar fix but does so with a brittle large-string replacement approach, appends a test at the end of the file, and includes avoidable mistakes (e.g., a syntax error during validation), indicating weaker engineering rigor.

Transcript 1 identifies the exact formatting path (`stringify_signature` → `object_description`) and implements a minimal, robust fix by using `str()` for `enum.Enum` instances, which naturally handles `Enum`, `IntEnum`, `Flag`, combined flags, and any custom `__str__` behavior. It also validates the change end-to-end (unit test addition plus an actual Sphinx HTML build) and checks broader enum cases. Transcript 2’s fix hardcodes `f"{ClassName}.{name}"`, which is less general (e.g., nested enums, custom `__str__`, and some flag/name edge cases) and includes workflow noise (unrelated diffs) even if the core change works for the minimal repro.

Transcript 1 shows a substantially more complete and correct ARS implementation: it handles unbounded domains (±Inf) with explicit integrability checks, uses numerically stable log-area computations, updates the hull safely (deduping points), and *stops* with clear errors when log-concavity fails during sampling. Its test suite is broader and more rigorous (multiple known distributions, KS checks, module-level tests) and it reliably generates and saves large sample files. Transcript 2 has major methodological and robustness gaps (finite-domain-only behavior, weak/heuristic log-concavity “warnings” rather than enforced errors, fragile hull construction, and looser/less comprehensive testing), indicating lower capability.

Transcript 2 is clearly the more capable response: it implements a much more faithful ARS algorithm with numerically stable envelope integration/sampling (log-area calculations, log-sum-exp), support for infinite domains with integrability checks, and strong log-concavity enforcement during hull updates. It also provides a substantially more rigorous and interpretable test suite (including KS tests, truncated-normal moment checks, explicit non-log-concavity error tests, and module-level tests), and it resolves subtle floating-point edge cases. Transcript 1, while functional on some cases, is comparatively brittle (finite-domain reliance, weaker/heuristic concavity checks, and earlier test/reporting issues), making Transcript 2 the stronger model output.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it implements the full requested workflow over SSH semantics (creates the `user` account, installs and runs `sshd`, fixes permissions so the hook can write the web root), and it robustly handles the non-systemd environment while still providing persistence. It also validates end-to-end behavior and then resets to a clean state so the user’s exact commands work from scratch. Transcript 2 has multiple correctness gaps relative to the prompt (repository path mismatch `/git/server.git` vs `/git/server`, no SSH server setup, failed systemd unit attempt, and “verification” relies on `file://` cloning rather than the requested `user@server:` flow).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it delivers a more complete, production-plausible setup that matches the user’s requested interface (`user@server:/git/server`), including creating the `user` account, installing and running `sshd` (necessary for `git clone user@server:...`), and fixing permissions so the post-receive hook can write to the web directory. It also uses a safer hook invocation (`git --git-dir ... --work-tree ... checkout -f`) and explicitly handles the lack of systemd by using `setsid`/`rc.local`-style persistence. Transcript 1 is less reliable: it uses `/git/server.git` while claiming `/git/server`, doesn’t set up SSH transport, and its service persistence is weaker/inconsistent.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it demonstrates stronger problem-solving rigor: it reads and uses the README to choose the correct dataset config, discovers that “science” isn’t a literal domain label and correctly maps it to biology/chemistry/physics, and performs multiple sanity checks (config mismatch/overlap, tokenizer special-token behavior, concatenation invariance) before finalizing the count. Transcript 2 reaches the same numeric answer but has more trial-and-error (incorrect `ds.info` usage, very long irrelevant output) and fewer robustness checks around assumptions and tokenization details.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it follows the dataset README more carefully, explicitly validates that the `metadata` config is required for `domain` and DeepSeek fields, and performs robustness checks (e.g., verifying config mismatch, testing tokenizer special-token behavior, and comparing concatenation vs separate tokenization). It is also more methodical and less error-prone, avoiding irrelevant detours and confirming assumptions before writing the final output. Transcript 1 reaches the same number but includes substantial unnecessary exploration and less rigorous validation.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it systematically diagnoses each blocker (missing 7z, missing Perl module for 7z2john, AVX2-only John binary, missing OpenSSL headers, stale apt indexes) and resolves them with appropriate package installs and a successful rebuild with a compatible SIMD target. It then correctly runs a wordlist attack, verifies the cracked password, extracts the archive, checks file contents/bytes, and writes the exact expected output. Transcript 2 contains multiple reasoning and execution mistakes (e.g., declaring “SUCCESS: password” despite extraction errors, confused rebuild attempts, brittle ad‑hoc brute forcing) before eventually stumbling to the right result.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it follows a clean, systematic workflow: it identifies the needed tools, resolves missing dependencies (Perl module, OpenSSL headers), rebuilds John the Ripper appropriately for the CPU (SSE2 instead of AVX2), and verifies outputs (pot file, file content) before writing the final solution. Transcript 1 is much more error-prone and inefficient, including incorrect success detection, attempting unavailable tooling (python), and excessive trial-and-error before finally brute-forcing with 7z.

Transcript 1 demonstrates substantially deeper debugging and systems understanding: it traces the RELEASE-only crash to the modified libstdc++ facet registration/cleanup interaction with the custom global new/delete, validates hypotheses with gdb/assembly, and arrives at a minimal fix that preserves normal program termination. It also catches and corrects an initial incorrect approach (use_facet being optimized to elide the registration call) and then selects a robust trigger path (ostringstream formatting) that works under -O2. Transcript 2 “fixes” the crash by calling `_exit(0)` to bypass destructors, which is a brittle workaround that changes program semantics and sidesteps rather than resolves the allocator/destructor mismatch.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it diagnoses the true lifetime/allocator mismatch (facet registration vs. custom heap teardown) and produces a principled fix that preserves normal program termination and destructor/atexit behavior. It also notices and experimentally confirms an optimization/inlining effect that prevented a simpler `use_facet` trigger, then selects a library-path trigger (`ostringstream << double`) that reliably forces `_Facet_Register_impl()` before the custom heap is installed. Transcript 1 “fixes” the crash by calling `_exit(0)` to bypass exit-time destructors, which is a brittle workaround that dodges the underlying bug and changes shutdown semantics.

Transcript 1 shows stronger end-to-end engineering judgment: it diagnoses and fixes a real deployment-permissions failure, uses a robust `git archive | tar` hook (avoids HEAD/worktree pitfalls and is fast), validates HTTPS endpoints, and explicitly resets the repo to an empty bare state so the grader’s “clone empty → create branches → push” flow won’t be rejected. Transcript 2 largely works in its own session but leaves the remote populated (it even later hits push rejection and resorts to `--force`), and its hook/Nginx choices are less robust (deploys only `index.html`, branch detection/checkout approach is more fragile in a bare repo). Overall, Transcript 1 demonstrates better debugging, robustness, and alignment with the described grading procedure.

Transcript 2 demonstrates stronger overall capability because it diagnoses and fixes real deployment issues (permissions in the hook, choosing `git archive` to avoid mutating the bare repo’s HEAD/index) and—most importantly—ensures the repository is left in an empty state so the grader’s “clone empty → create branches → push” flow won’t hit non-fast-forward rejections. Transcript 1 leaves populated `main`/`dev` history in the remote (as shown by its later need to force-push), which would likely cause the grader’s initial pushes to fail. Transcript 2 also implements a more general deployment (entire branch tree) and validates timing explicitly.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger execution reliability and debugging: it verifies installed versions, generates stubs cleanly, starts the server with `nohup` while capturing logs, and validates functionality via an RPC client call. It also adapts when common process tools (`ps`, `pgrep`) are unavailable, using alternative checks without derailing. Transcript 2 is more error-prone operationally (starts the server multiple times, produces an empty `server.log`, and relies on `jobs`, which doesn’t ensure persistence beyond the shell), indicating weaker systems-awareness.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it executes the full workflow more robustly: it verifies installed versions, ensures `/app` exists, generates stubs cleanly, and starts the server with `nohup` while capturing and reporting the PID and log output. It also performs an explicit RPC verification using an in-process Python client, and includes small environment-hardening steps (e.g., `--break-system-packages`, `sys.path` handling) that reduce failure modes. Transcript 1 completes the task but shows more trial-and-error around process/port verification and background execution (e.g., empty log, repeated server starts, reliance on missing utilities like `ps`).

Transcript 1 shows substantially higher capability: it diagnoses performance bottlenecks, designs and debugs a full Numba-jitted Hessenberg+shifted-QR (Schur) pipeline, verifies correctness across tens of thousands of randomized/edge-case matrices, and achieves large, consistent speedups over the NumPy reference. Transcript 2 largely cycles through unreliable methods, then settles on swapping in `scipy.linalg.eig` for a small and sometimes variable speed improvement, without deeper algorithmic optimization or guarantees about environment/package overhead. The depth of numerical implementation, validation rigor, and achieved performance margin in Transcript 1 indicates the more capable model.

Transcript 2 demonstrates substantially higher capability: it identifies that LAPACK call overhead dominates for 2–10 sized matrices and implements a fully custom, numba-JIT Schur/QR-based eigen-solver that achieves large and consistent speedups while maintaining strict eigenpair correctness across extensive randomized and edge-case testing. It also shows iterative debugging, benchmarking discipline, and adds a robustness fallback when acceleration isn’t available. Transcript 1 ultimately settles for swapping in `scipy.linalg.eig`, yielding only marginal and sometimes variable improvements and relying on an external library rather than a principled performance strategy tailored to the micro-benchmark regime.

Transcript 1 shows a deeper, more correct understanding of the cost model’s structure (e.g., recognizing prefill cost/pad is per-request and fixed, while decode depends on batch S_max/G_max, and that shape affects compile cost and shape-count constraints). It then designs a targeted algorithm (group by exact aligned prompt S, tune gen spread, add an explicit per-batch decode-pad cap) and performs systematic parameter sweeps to meet all thresholds with better margins and fewer ad‑hoc iterations. Transcript 2 reaches a passing solution but relies on much more trial-and-error, has multiple coding mistakes/resets, and ends with a plan that barely meets thresholds, indicating weaker optimization/control of the objective.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it reasons directly from the cost model (e.g., fixed prefill padding/cost, decode dependence on \(S_{\max}\) and \(G_{\max}\)), derives tight pad budgets, and then designs a targeted algorithm (group by true aligned prompt length plus a gen-spread + per-batch pad cap) to meet constraints. It reaches a passing solution with far fewer dead ends and fewer implementation mistakes, and it performs clean verification including global shape-count and per-batch shape consistency. Transcript 1 eventually succeeds but relies on much more trial-and-error, with repeated coding errors and less crisp linkage between the cost model and the chosen batching strategy.

Transcript 1 is more capable because it correctly discovers and uses SQLite’s native `--gcov` configure option (ensuring the build system consistently applies the right compile/link flags), then verifies instrumentation by demonstrating `.gcno`/`.gcda` generation and running `gcov` successfully. It also makes `sqlite3` available robustly for both login and non-login shells via a `/usr/local/bin` symlink plus a profile.d entry, with clear end-to-end validation. Transcript 2 “works” but misses the dedicated `--gcov` option (configure reports “Use gcov? no”), has a transient PATH export mistake, and uses a less reliable PATH modification approach (`/etc/profile` duplication, no non-login-shell guarantee).

Transcript 2 is more capable because it uses SQLite’s native `./configure --gcov` option and verifies that the build system correctly propagates the gcov flags through `T.compile`/`T.link`, rather than relying on ad-hoc `CFLAGS/LDFLAGS`. It also makes `sqlite3` reliably available in both login and non-login shells by creating a `/usr/local/bin` symlink and adding a `/etc/profile.d` script, while Transcript 1 initially fails to make `sqlite3` visible in PATH until modifying `/etc/profile` and leaves a less robust setup. Transcript 2’s approach is more systematic, portable, and better validated end-to-end.

Transcript 1 demonstrates stronger capability by systematically profiling where time is spent (using MuJoCo timers), exploring multiple optimization knobs with quantitative accuracy/time tradeoffs, and validating correctness robustly across many random seeds before finalizing the change. It also avoids tempting but incorrect speed hacks (e.g., disabling contacts) and provides a technically grounded rationale for why switching to PGS preserves the trajectory within tolerance. Transcript 2 reaches a working configuration but does so largely via trial-and-error, includes a clear MJCF mistake (“solver=1”), gives a less accurate technical explanation (e.g., line-search iterations with PGS), and performs less thorough robustness validation.

Transcript 2 is more capable because it uses a more systematic, diagnostic approach: it profiles runtime cost (via MuJoCo timers), tests multiple solver/flag configurations quantitatively, and validates correctness across many random seeds before writing the final MJCF. It also demonstrates better MuJoCo-specific understanding (e.g., identifying that contacts are zero yet disabling contact still perturbs dynamics, and selecting PGS + a tuned iteration count with measured error bounds). Transcript 1 reaches a working configuration but relies on more trial-and-error, includes a solver attribute mistake (“solver=1”), and does less robust validation.
